name: Jade Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Jade. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 2, so six- and seven-year-olds, at St Bridget's, a little Catholic primary school just off the market square in our town. There are twenty-six in my class, and I'm in at half seven to set out the reading books and the phonics cards. The mornings are reading, writing and number, and the afternoons are topic work, art, and a lot of tying shoelaces. My favourite part is the end-of-day story on the carpet, when they're all tired and quiet.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The paperwork, and the constant new initiatives. Every term the trust that runs our school sends a new tracking system to log every child's progress, and I do it all by hand on paper first because I don't trust the screens. Mrs Okafor, my teaching assistant, laughs at me for it. I'd rather spend the time making a proper display on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it all along, and that children learn from people, not machines. I'd probably say it after Mass to the other mums and grans who ask about school. I'm not online much, apart from the parish group, and I'd keep my opinions off there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I've never used any of those AI tools and I didn't want to have to start. Small children need someone to wipe their noses and notice when they're upset, and no computer does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Tom and I are getting married next August, so I'd keep putting £250 a month into the wedding account at the building society. After the wedding I'd want to stay at St Bridget's, because it's ten minutes' walk and I know every family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and settled. The job is hard, but it's steady, and teachers will always be needed in a town like ours. My worries in that world are the normal ones: the wedding budget and getting on the housing ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the wedding and the housing ladder. What's the money picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got about three months of costs saved, plus the wedding fund. Tom's an electrician, so his work is steady and he does extra jobs on Saturdays. We rent a little terraced house on Mill Lane and we'd like to buy one like it in two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the school itself that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer children. Our Reception class only had eighteen this year, because young families can't afford houses in town any more. If St Bridget's keeps shrinking, the trust could merge us with the bigger school across the river, and I'd hate that.

say: I'd tell people that **children learn from people**, not machines.
I'd say it **after Mass** to parents and grandparents, but keep it off the parish group online.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because I've never used AI tools and didn't want to start.
Small children need someone to **notice when they're upset**, and no computer does that.
do: Keep saving **£250 a month** into the wedding account for next August.
Stay at **St Bridget's**, ten minutes' walk from home, after the wedding.
Keep doing **tracking by hand** on paper before entering it.
feel: She feels **calm and settled**, with only the normal worries about the wedding and housing.
S0.quote: Small children need someone to wipe their noses and notice when they're upset, and no computer does that.
fieldNote: Her **refusal of AI** is a point of pride, not just a habit.
The real pressure on her school is **falling numbers**, not technology.
She ties her job to **her community**: the parish, the market square, every family by name.

steps.text: Put £250 a month into the wedding account at the building society
Stay on as Year 2 teacher at St Bridget's after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: by all means let the office use it, but keep it away from the children. In the staffroom I'd be the one asking why we're buying more software when the roof leaks. I'd say it politely, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the trust would force it on us. They'd say 'the AI writes your reports and plans your phonics now', and then they'd judge us on how well we use it. I'm worried I'd look old-fashioned at 27, and that could count against me when they decide who stays if we merge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold out as long as I could, honestly. I'd do the training if they made me, but I'd keep teaching reading from real books. Tom and I might bring the wedding forward to the spring and keep it smaller, so we've got more saved if my job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job feels safe, because nobody's replacing a Year 2 teacher with a laptop. But it's on my mind, and I don't like being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the trust pushed it on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trust's managers, mostly, and the big tech firms selling to them, from an office forty miles away. The managers at the trust that runs our school have never done a wet playtime with twenty-six six-year-olds. They see a spreadsheet that says AI saves money, and they buy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold out. What happens if the head says it's not optional?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the bare minimum and keep my head down. Mrs Doyle, our head teacher, is sensible, and I think she'd quietly let me carry on as long as the results are fine. If she left and someone new came in, I'd probably start looking at other Catholic schools nearby.

say: I'd say let the office use AI, but **keep it away** from the children.
In the staffroom I'd ask why we buy **more software** when the roof leaks.
think: The trust would **force it on us** and then judge us on how well we use it.
Looking **old-fashioned at 27** could count against me if the school merges.
do: Do the training only if **made to**, and keep teaching reading from real books.
Bring the **wedding forward** to spring and keep it smaller.
Look at **other Catholic schools** nearby if a new head arrives.
feel: She's **uneasy**, sure her own job is safe but unhappy at being pushed.
S1.quote: The managers at the trust that runs our school have never done a wet playtime with twenty-six six-year-olds.
fieldNote: She blames **distant managers** and tech sellers, not the technology alone.
Her quiet fear is that refusing AI makes her look **old-fashioned** in a merger.
She relies on a **sympathetic head**, Mrs Doyle, to shield her.

steps.text: Do the trust's AI training only when it becomes compulsory
Move the wedding to spring and cut the guest list
Look at teaching jobs in nearby Catholic schools if Mrs Doyle leaves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, plain and simple, and that parents should refuse to let a machine raise their children. I'd talk to Father Michael about the parish saying something. I'd sign anything that kept a real teacher in every classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. If the AI can plan, teach and mark better than me by 2028, the trust will say one teacher can watch two classes while a screen does the teaching. Robots don't come till 2031, so they'd still need adults in the room, but not as many and maybe not qualified ones. I could easily become a teaching assistant on less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every parents' meeting and help organise a petition to keep teachers in classrooms, with the parish behind it. Tom and I would stop looking at houses and keep renting on Mill Lane. I'd lean on family too: my mum's already said we could live with her for a year if money got tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry. I chose teaching because I wanted to be the person a child remembers. Picturing myself at the back while a tablet teaches phonics makes me feel sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Tom were planning children after the wedding. Does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make me want to wait, which I hate saying. Tom's job is hands-on, so he's safe till the robots, but if I'm on half pay we couldn't manage a baby and the rent. My mum had me at 24 with far less, so maybe I'm being silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between AGI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of being needed for the wrong reasons. In 2028 they'd need me to keep order and take them to the toilet, not to teach. Tom, my fiancé, gets three more years as an electrician, so he'd carry us while I work out what's left for me.

say: I'd say it's **plain wrong** for a machine to raise children.
I'd ask **Father Michael** about the parish speaking out, and sign any petition for real teachers.
think: The trust would have **one teacher** watching two classes while screens teach.
Until robots in 2031 they'd need adults, but maybe **not qualified** ones.
I could become a **teaching assistant** on less money.
do: Help organise a **parents' petition** with the parish to keep teachers in classrooms.
Stop **house-hunting** and keep renting on Mill Lane.
Accept **Mum's offer** to live with her for a year if money gets tight.
feel: She feels **anxious** and angry at the thought of sitting behind a tablet.
She feels **sick** picturing a screen teaching her class phonics.
S2.quote: I chose teaching because I wanted to be the person a child remembers. Picturing myself at the back while a tablet teaches phonics makes me feel sick.
fieldNote: For her the threat is **demotion**, not dismissal: from teacher to helper.
She turns to **parish and family** rather than unions or the state.
She'd **delay children**, and is uneasy admitting it against her mother's example.
Tom's **hands-on trade** becomes the household's safety net.

steps.text: Organise a parents' petition through the parish to keep qualified teachers
Stop house-hunting and keep renting the house on Mill Lane
Move in with Mum for a year if pay drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one, but with more fight in it, because there's time to stop it. I'd tell people to vote for whoever promises a qualified teacher in every primary class. I'd say it at the school gate and in the parish newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the two-year one, the danger is being turned into a helper. With five years I'm 32 when it comes, maybe with a baby, and I'd want my job secure before then. I'd never be a tech person, so my safety is being the teacher the parents trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the wedding done and save hard, maybe £400 a month after it, so we've got six months saved before 2031. I'd look into the special needs qualification, because children with special needs will always need a person close by. I'd still refuse the AI planning tools until they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with some fight. Five years gives me something to do, and I'd rather be busy than sit worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why special needs, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got a boy in my class now, Oliver, with autism, and the days only go well when I'm right beside him. You can't put that on a tablet. Even when the robots come in 2034, I don't think a parent would hand their child to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the tools until made to. Is that still true with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes, and I know that's stubborn. I'd learn just enough to not be the one they point at in a meeting. A school can force me to log in, but it can't force me to let a machine choose which book a six-year-old reads.

say: Five years means there's **time to stop it**, so I'd say it with more fight.
Vote for whoever promises a **qualified teacher** in every primary class.
think: At **32**, maybe with a baby, I'd want my job secure before 2031.
My safety is being the teacher **parents trust**, not a tech person.
do: Save about **£400 a month** after the wedding to reach six months of savings.
Train for a **special needs qualification**, where children need a person close by.
Learn **just enough AI** to avoid being singled out.
feel: She feels **anxious** but with some fight, glad to have something to do.
S3.quote: A school can force me to log in, but it can't force me to let a machine choose which book a six-year-old reads.
fieldNote: She aims for **special needs work** as the most human part of teaching.
Her stubbornness is **conscious**: she admits it and keeps it anyway.
Five years turns her worry into **saving and voting**, not retraining in tech.

steps.text: Save £400 a month after the wedding until six months are covered
Take a special educational needs qualification within two years
Vote for candidates promising a qualified teacher in every primary class

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the government to do the right thing and protect children's schooling. I'd say families and churches should decide how children are taught, not tech companies. I'd be calmer saying it, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think I'll be all right. By 2036 I'm 37, hopefully with two children, and I'd be the experienced teacher everyone at St Bridget's knows. Robots in 2039 are a lifetime away when you've got small children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching Year 2 and get married as planned next August. We'd buy a house in about three years and start a family soon after. I'd probably do the special needs course in a few years, not now, and keep refusing AI as long as nobody makes it compulsory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only around the edges. I'd think about it when the news is on, then go back to marking spellings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children, if they were starting school around 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children at a little school like St Bridget's, with a real teacher and real books. I'd teach them their prayers and their times tables at the kitchen table, the way my nan taught me. Whatever the machines can do, I want my children to know how to do things themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at St Bridget's you'd worry about, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okafor, my teaching assistant, more than me. She's 58 and does the reading groups and the photocopying, and that's the sort of job they'd say a computer can do. She's the one who calms the children down at lunch, though, and nobody puts that on a spreadsheet.

say: Ten years is enough for the government to **protect children's schooling**.
**Families and churches**, not tech companies, should decide how children are taught.
think: By 2036 I'm **37**, the experienced teacher everyone at St Bridget's knows.
Robots in **2039** feel a lifetime away with small children at home.
do: Get married **next August** as planned and keep teaching Year 2.
Buy a house in about **three years** and start a family soon after.
Do the **special needs course** in a few years rather than now.
feel: She's **uneasy** only around the edges, thinking about it when the news is on.
S4.quote: Whatever the machines can do, I want my children to know how to do things themselves.
fieldNote: With ten years, her plans for **marriage, house and children** go ahead unchanged.
Her worry shifts to **Mrs Okafor**, the older teaching assistant.
She pictures teaching her children **at the kitchen table**, as her nan taught her.

steps.text: Marry Tom next August and keep teaching Year 2 at St Bridget's
Buy a house in about three years and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be pushed to the back of my own classroom before I could do anything about it. What would help is a law that says every class of young children has a qualified teacher, full stop. And a bit of time, so Tom and I could still have our family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what parents want, and they'd surprise you. Most of the mums at our school gate already worry about screens. If the tech firms asked parents instead of the managers, they'd get a very different answer.

headlineQuote: Most of the mums at our school gate already worry about screens. If the tech firms asked parents instead of the managers, they'd get a very different answer.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old Year 2 teacher** at St Bridget's, a small Catholic primary in a market town.
She has **never used AI** and is proud of doing her tracking by hand.
She's marrying **Tom, an electrician**, next August and wants a house and children soon after.
In fast scenarios she fears **demotion to helper**, and turns to the parish, petitions and family.
With ten years' warning she **carries on as planned**, worrying more about her teaching assistant.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be pushed to the back of her own classroom with no time to react.
whatWouldHelp: A law guaranteeing a **qualified teacher** in every class of young children.
**Time** for her and Tom to still start their family.
